title: Khoresh karafs
subtitle: Persian celery and herb stew with lamb
excerpt: Khoresh karafs is a Persian braised celery stew with lamb and large amounts of fresh parsley and mint. The celery becomes very tender in the long braise and the herbs give a bright, fresh flavour that lifts what could otherwise be a heavy winter stew.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Khoresh karafs documented as a classic home khoresh. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). The large herb quantity and the importance of fresh mint described.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat gently.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Make a large pot and freeze in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The stew is better made the day before. The flavours deepen and mellow overnight.

content.text: Khoresh karafs is a Persian braised stew of lamb, celery, and fresh herbs. The celery is cut into short pieces and braises low and slow until completely tender. Large amounts of parsley and mint are added partway through cooking; they soften but keep a vivid green colour and fragrance. Served over chelow, it is a light but deeply flavoured winter dish.

items.prepNote: cut into 3 cm pieces, leaves reserved

content.text: Heat {{olive-oil}} in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Add {{onion}} and cook for ten minutes until golden. Stir in {{turmeric-ground}} and cook for one minute.
Add {{lamb-shoulder}} and brown well on all sides, five to seven minutes. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} and {{black-pepper}}.
Add 500 ml of water and bring to the boil. Reduce to a low simmer, cover, and cook for 30 minutes.
Add {{celery}} pieces and cook covered for another 30 minutes.

Add {{parsley-flat}}, {{mint}}, and lemon juice from {{lemon}}. Stir, cover, and cook for a further 20 minutes until the lamb is very tender and the celery is soft. Taste and adjust seasoning. The stew should have some liquid but not be watery.

items.symptom: The celery is still crunchy after an hour
items.cause: Heat too low or not enough liquid
items.fix: Add another 100 ml of water and increase the heat slightly. Celery takes at least 45 minutes to become properly tender in a braise.

items.cause: Herbs added too early and overcooked
items.fix: Add a handful of fresh parsley and mint at the very end and stir through just before serving. This refreshes the herb note.
Start with half the lemon juice. The sourness should be present but subtle. Add more at the end if needed.

items.symptom: The lamb is still tough at the one-hour mark
items.cause: Lamb shoulder varies in size and age
items.fix: Continue cooking covered. Lamb shoulder needs the collagen to break down: give it another 20 to 30 minutes on a low simmer.

content.text: Karafs is the Persian word for celery, and khoresh karafs is a home favourite rather than a restaurant dish. It is one of the lighter khoresh in Persian cooking, valued in spring when celery is at its best. Celery paired with lamb and herbs is unusual in Western cooking but common in Persian cuisine, which uses vegetables in ways that European traditions do not. Mint is the key herb: it lifts the earthiness of the celery and the richness of the lamb into something aromatic and fresh.
